The Art of Stealth

Minimizing Traces and Blending In

What is Stealth?

Stealth is the practice of minimizing detectable traces and blending malicious activity with legitimate system operations to avoid detection.

  • •Minimize forensic artifacts like unusual file timestamps or logs.
  • •Blend in with legitimate system activity, processes, and network traffic.
  • •Evade detection by security tools, analysts, and automated monitoring.
Key Takeaway

Effective stealth allows for prolonged access and deeper system compromise without triggering alarms, crucial for advanced penetration testing.

screens.title: Timestomping on Linux
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most effective stealth techniques is timestomping, which involves manipulating the creation, modification, and access timestamps of files. This is crucial because forensic analysts often look for recently created or modified files as indicators of compromise. By making your malicious files appear older or match the timestamps of legitimate system files, you can significantly hinder detection. On Linux, the touch command is your primary tool for this. While touch is commonly used to update a file's access and modification times to the current time, its -r option allows you to reference another file's timestamps. This means you can take a legitimate system binary, like slash bin slash ls, and apply its exact timestamps to your malicious script or executable. This makes your file blend in, appearing as if it's been part of the system for as long as the reference file, making it much harder for an analyst to spot it as a recent addition. Remember, the goal is to make your artifacts look as benign and aged as possible. Timestomping on Linux means timestomping alters file metadata to obscure the true creation or modification time of malicious artifacts, making them harder to spot.. In practical terms, manipulating file timestamps with `touch`. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 11›Chapter 10.9›Timestomping on Linux
Technique Deep Dive

Timestomping on Linux

Manipulating File Timestamps with touch

  • •Modify creation, modification, and access times of files.
  • •Evade forensic analysis by making malicious files appear legitimate.
  • •Use touch -r to reference timestamps from benign system files.
Example Scenario

You've deployed a backdoor script. To hide its recent creation, you match its timestamps to an old, trusted system binary like /bin/ls.

Key Takeaway

Timestomping on Linux with touch -r is a simple yet powerful way to obscure the true age of malicious files, hindering forensic efforts.

# Create a dummy file
touch /tmp/evil.sh

# Verify initial timestamps (example output)
stat /tmp/evil.sh
# Access: 2023-10-27 10:00:00.000000000 +0000
# Modify: 2023-10-27 10:00:00.000000000 +0000
# Change: 2023-10-27 10:00:00.000000000 +0000

# Change creation/modification time to match /bin/ls
touch -r /bin/ls /tmp/evil.sh

# Verify new timestamps (will match /bin/ls)
stat /tmp/evil.sh
# Access: 2022-01-15 08:30:00.000000000 +0000 (example)
# Modify: 2022-01-15 08:30:00.000000000 +0000 (example)
# Change: 2023-10-27 10:01:00.000000000 +0000 (current time)
Explanation

The touch -r command copies the reference file's access and modification times. Note that the 'Change' (inode modification) time will still update, but this is less commonly scrutinized than access/modification times for file age.

screens.title: Timestomping on Windows
screens.narratorSegment: Just as on Linux, timestomping is a vital stealth technique on Windows to obscure the true age of your malicious files. Windows systems also record creation, modification, and access times, and these can be powerful indicators for forensic investigators. PowerShell provides a flexible and powerful way to manipulate these timestamps programmatically. You can use the Get-Item cmdlet to retrieve the timestamp properties of a legitimate system file, such as notepad. exe, which has likely been on the system since its installation. Once you have these reference timestamps, you can then apply them to your malicious executable or script using the same Get-Item cmdlet to select your target file, and then directly assign the Creation Time, Last Write Time, and Last Access Time properties. This makes your payload appear as if it's an integral, long-standing part of the operating system, significantly increasing its chances of evading detection during a forensic review. It's a subtle but highly effective way to blend in. Module 11›Chapter 10.9›Timestomping on Windows
Technique Deep Dive

Timestomping on Windows

Using PowerShell to Modify File Timestamps

  • •Windows tracks CreationTime, LastWriteTime, and LastAccessTime.
  • •PowerShell allows direct manipulation of these file properties.
  • •Match timestamps to legitimate system binaries like notepad.exe.
Example Scenario

After dropping malicious.exe, you modify its timestamps to match notepad.exe, making it appear as an old, trusted system file.

Key Takeaway

PowerShell provides precise control over file timestamps on Windows, enabling attackers to effectively hide the age of their malicious payloads from forensic scrutiny.

# Get the timestamp of a legitimate file
$refFile = Get-Item C:\Windows\System32
otepad.exe
$creationTime = $refFile.CreationTime
$lastWriteTime = $refFile.LastWriteTime
$lastAccessTime = $refFile.LastAccessTime

# Apply to your malicious file
$malFile = Get-Item C:\ProgramData\malicious.exe
$malFile.CreationTime = $creationTime
$malFile.LastWriteTime = $lastWriteTime
$malFile.LastAccessTime = $lastAccessTime

# Verify new timestamps (example output)
Get-Item C:\ProgramData\malicious.exe | Select-Object CreationTime, LastWriteTime, LastAccessTime
# CreationTime   : 1/15/2022 8:30:00 AM
# LastWriteTime  : 1/15/2022 8:30:00 AM
# LastAccessTime : 1/15/2022 8:30:00 AM
Explanation

This script first captures the timestamps from a trusted system file. Then, it applies those exact timestamps to your malicious file, making it appear as if it was created or modified at the same time as the legitimate reference file.

screens.title: Understanding Userland Rootkits
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond manipulating timestamps, userland rootkits offer a more sophisticated way to achieve stealth by actively hiding your malicious presence. Unlike complex kernel-mode rootkits, which operate at the core of the operating system, userland rootkits work by modifying user-mode libraries. This means they intercept and alter the behavior of standard A P I functions that user-level tools rely on. For instance, if you want to hide a malicious file or directory, a userland rootkit might hook the readdir function, which is used by commands like ls to list directory contents. When readdir is called, the rootkit filters out any entries matching your hidden file or process, making it invisible to the user. On Linux, this is often achieved using LD underscore PRELOAD, which forces a custom library to be loaded before others, allowing it to override standard functions. On Windows, similar effects can be achieved through DLL injection. The key takeaway is that userland rootkits provide a powerful layer of concealment, making it extremely difficult for an analyst using standard tools to detect your hidden artifacts. Understanding Userland Rootkits means userland rootkits intercept and modify standard library calls to filter out malicious entries, effectively making them invisible to common system utilities.. In practical terms, hiding malicious activity from user-level tools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Establishing Persistence
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've gained initial access and established stealth, the next critical phase is persistence. Persistence is the ability to maintain your access to a compromised system across various disruptions, such as reboots, user logoffs, or even system updates. Without persistence, all your hard work in gaining initial access could be undone with a simple system restart, forcing you to start from scratch. This is why it's a cornerstone of advanced penetration testing. Attackers need to ensure they can regain control whenever necessary, often without requiring user interaction. This involves embedding malicious code or configurations into legitimate system mechanisms that automatically execute at startup, logon, or specific intervals. For example, a scheduled task on Windows or a cron job on Linux can ensure your payload runs every time the system boots. Understanding and implementing robust persistence mechanisms is what differentiates a one-time compromise from a long-term, strategic foothold within a target environment. What is Persistence?

Persistence is the ability to maintain access to a compromised system across reboots, user logoffs, or other system events.

  • •Guarantees continued access even after system disruptions.
  • •Crucial for long-term objectives and simulating real-world attacks.

Key Takeaway

System Reboot

Why it Matters

screens.title: Scheduled Tasks for Windows Persistence
screens.narratorSegment: On Windows, scheduled tasks are one of the most common and effective methods for establishing persistence. They allow you to configure programs or scripts to run at specific times, intervals, or in response to particular system events, such as a user logging on or the system starting up. The schtasks command-line utility is your primary interface for creating and managing these tasks. When creating a malicious scheduled task, it's crucial to use benign-sounding names and paths to blend in with legitimate system tasks. Windows Persistence

Scheduled Tasks for Windows Persistence

Automating Payload Execution with schtasks

  • •Run payloads at specific times, intervals, or events (e.g., startup, logon).
  • •Use schtasks /create to configure new tasks.
  • •Crucial to use benign task names and run with SYSTEM privileges.
Common Mistake

Using easily identifiable task names like "Backdoor" or "Persistence". Always blend in with legitimate system names.

Scheduled tasks are a versatile and powerful Windows persistence method, especially when configured with stealthy names and SYSTEM privileges.

# Create a task to run 'malicious.exe' every day at 09:00
schtasks /create /tn "MyMaliciousTask" /tr "C:\ProgramData\malicious.exe" /sc daily /st 09:00 /ru System
# /tn: Task Name (e.g., "Microsoft\Windows\SystemMaintenance\SystemUpdater")
# /tr: Task Run (path to your payload)
# /sc: Schedule Type (e.g., daily, onlogon, onstart)
# /st: Start Time (if applicable)
# /ru: Run As User (e.g., System for high privileges)

# Example: Stealthy task running at logon as SYSTEM
schtasks /create /tn "Microsoft\Windows\SystemMaintenance\SystemUpdater" /tr "C:\ProgramData\SystemUpdater.exe" /sc onlogon /ru System /rl highest /f
# /rl highest: Runs with highest available privileges
# /f: Forces task creation if name exists
Explanation

This command creates a scheduled task. The second example demonstrates a more stealthy approach by mimicking a legitimate Microsoft path and running at logon with SYSTEM privileges, which is highly effective for persistence.

screens.title: Creating Stealthy Hidden Users
screens.narratorSegment: Another advanced Windows persistence technique involves creating a new user account and then manipulating the registry to hide it from standard enumeration tools. This provides a covert backdoor that can be used to regain access without being easily discovered by security analysts. The process begins by creating a new user account using the net user command, assigning it a strong password. Next, you'll want to add this user to the Administrators group using net localgroup to ensure it has elevated privileges. The crucial stealth step comes next: hiding the user. This is achieved by modifying a specific registry key, HKLM backslash SOFTWARE backslash Microsoft backslash Windows NT backslash Current Version backslash Winlogon backslash Special Accounts backslash User List. By creating a new DWORD value under this key with the username and setting its value to zero, you effectively remove the user from the login screen and the output of net user commands. This makes the account invisible to casual inspection, providing a highly stealthy and persistent access point. However, remember that not hiding the user is a common mistake that makes this method easily discoverable.

Linux Persistence

Cron Jobs for Linux Persistence

Scheduling Malicious Tasks with crontab

  • •Automate commands or scripts at specified times or intervals.
  • •The @reboot directive ensures execution at system startup.
  • •Modify user's crontab using (crontab -l; echo ...) | crontab -.
Safety Note

Ensure your persistent script is stealthy, doesn't leave obvious logs, and uses hidden file names to avoid detection.

Key Takeaway

Cron jobs are a reliable and widely available method for achieving persistence on Linux, particularly useful for ensuring payloads run after reboots.

# View current user's crontab entries
crontab -l
# (No output if empty)

# Add a cron job to run a Python script at every reboot
(crontab -l; echo "@reboot /usr/bin/python3 /tmp/.hidden_backdoor.py") | crontab -

# Verify the new entry
crontab -l
# @reboot /usr/bin/python3 /tmp/.hidden_backdoor.py

# Example: Run every 5 minutes
(crontab -l; echo "*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/python3 /tmp/.hidden_backdoor.py") | crontab -
Explanation

The command pipes the existing crontab entries and a new @reboot entry into crontab -, which updates the user's cron schedule. This ensures the specified Python script executes every time the system reboots.

Modern and Traditional Linux Autostart

After=network.target

Welcome to a crucial chapter in advanced penetration testing: Post-Exploitation Stealth and Persistence. Gaining initial access to a system is a significant achievement, but it's often just the beginning. To truly simulate real-world attacker behavior and achieve long-term objectives, you must master the art of remaining undetected and ensuring your access endures. This involves minimizing forensic artifacts and blending your malicious activities with legitimate system operations, which we call 'stealth.' Simultaneously, you need to establish 'persistence,' guaranteeing that your access to the system remains even after reboots, user logoffs, or other system disruptions. Throughout this chapter, we'll explore the fundamental concepts and practical techniques that enable you to operate covertly and maintain control within compromised environments, transforming initial access into sustained strategic advantage. Post-Exploitation Stealth & Persistence means initial system compromise is just the beginning. true mastery lies in maintaining a covert presence and ensuring continuous access, even after system reboots.. In practical terms, mastering undetected access and long-term control. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. In this section, we'll outline the key learning objectives that will guide your journey through post-exploitation stealth and persistence. These objectives are designed to build your practical skills, enabling you to not only understand the theoretical concepts but also to apply them effectively in real-world penetration testing scenarios. You'll begin by grasping the fundamental importance of remaining undetected and maintaining access, which forms the bedrock of advanced operations. We'll then dive into specific techniques, starting with how to manipulate file timestamps to evade forensic detection. You'll also learn about userland rootkits, a powerful method for concealing malicious activity from standard system tools, and explore initial Windows persistence mechanisms like scheduled tasks, services, and registry run keys. Each objective is a step towards becoming a more sophisticated and effective penetration tester.

Continuing our exploration, these next objectives will further refine your capabilities in maintaining covert control. You'll learn to implement robust Linux persistence mechanisms, which are essential for multi-platform engagements. This includes mastering cron jobs, a classic method for scheduling tasks, and understanding how to leverage modern Systemd services for boot-time execution. We'll also delve into the more advanced Windows persistence techniques, specifically focusing on how to create and effectively hide user accounts and manipulate registry entries to ensure stealthy, long-term access. Finally, we'll analyze common mistakes and crucial safety notes associated with persistence, ensuring you can apply these techniques responsibly and effectively, minimizing the risk of detection and maximizing your operational security. These skills are vital for any professional penetration tester. Deepening Your Expertise means by achieving these objectives, you will gain the ability to implement sophisticated techniques for hidden access and long-term system control.. In practical terms, advanced techniques for covert operations. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. Stealth is a fundamental principle in post-exploitation, focusing on minimizing your forensic footprint and blending your malicious activities with legitimate system operations. The goal is to avoid detection by security analysts, automated tools, and forensic investigations. Think of it like a chameleon changing its colors to match its surroundings; your malicious files, processes, and network connections should appear as normal as possible. This involves techniques that obscure your presence, making it difficult for defenders to differentiate between legitimate system behavior and your covert actions. For example, if you create a new file, you wouldn't want its creation timestamp to immediately flag it as suspicious. Instead, you'd want it to look like it's been there for a while, perhaps matching the age of other system files. Mastering stealth is crucial because it allows you to maintain access for longer periods, gather more intelligence, and achieve your objectives without raising alarms, ultimately increasing the success rate of your penetration test. The Art of Stealth means stealth ensures your presence on a compromised system remains undetected, crucial for long-term access and avoiding forensic analysis.. In practical terms, minimizing traces and blending in. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One of the most effective stealth techniques is timestomping, which involves manipulating the creation, modification, and access timestamps of files. This is crucial because forensic analysts often look for recently created or modified files as indicators of compromise. By making your malicious files appear older or match the timestamps of legitimate system files, you can significantly hinder detection. On Linux, the touch command is your primary tool for this. While touch is commonly used to update a file's access and modification times to the current time, its -r option allows you to reference another file's timestamps. This means you can take a legitimate system binary, like slash bin slash ls, and apply its exact timestamps to your malicious script or executable. This makes your file blend in, appearing as if it's been part of the system for as long as the reference file, making it much harder for an analyst to spot it as a recent addition. Remember, the goal is to make your artifacts look as benign and aged as possible. Timestomping on Linux means timestomping alters file metadata to obscure the true creation or modification time of malicious artifacts, making them harder to spot.. In practical terms, manipulating file timestamps with `touch`. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Just as on Linux, timestomping is a vital stealth technique on Windows to obscure the true age of your malicious files. Windows systems also record creation, modification, and access times, and these can be powerful indicators for forensic investigators. PowerShell provides a flexible and powerful way to manipulate these timestamps programmatically. As we conclude this chapter, let's recap the essential concepts of post-exploitation stealth and persistence. These two principles are foundational for any advanced penetration tester aiming to achieve long-term objectives within a compromised environment. Stealth is all about minimizing your digital footprint and blending your malicious activities with legitimate system operations to avoid detection. It's the art of being present without being seen. Persistence, on the other hand, ensures that your hard-won access to a system remains intact, even after disruptions like reboots or user logoffs. It's about building a resilient foothold. A key technique for achieving stealth is timestomping, where you manipulate file timestamps to make your malicious files appear older and less suspicious to forensic analysts.
